title: Regular -er verbs
description: Conjugate everyday -er verbs in the present, including their spelling changes.

guide.summary: Almost every French verb you meet ends in -er, and they all work the same way: cut off -er and add one of six endings. This page has the endings, the small spelling changes that protect the sound, and the two ways aimer is used.

sections.title: The six endings
sections.text: Remove -er from the infinitive to get the stem, then add the ending for your subject. The endings -e, -es and -ent are silent, so parle, parles and parlent all sound the same.
steps: Find the subject: who is doing it?
Remove -er from the infinitive to get the stem.
Add the ending written on that subject’s row.
Never use -ont here: ont and sont belong to avoir and être.

examples.fr: J’habite à Lyon et je travaille ici.
examples.en: I live in Lyon and I work here.

examples.fr: Mes parents habitent à la campagne.
examples.en: My parents live in the country.

watch: Hearing nothing at the end does not mean writing nothing: il regarde and ils regardent sound the same.
-ez goes only with vous, -ons only with nous.
A noun subject counts as il/elle or ils/elles: mes parents takes the ils ending.

sections.title: Je or j’?
sections.text: Je keeps its e in front of a consonant and loses it in front of a vowel sound. A silent h counts as a vowel sound.
steps: Look at the first letter of the verb, not at its meaning.
A, e, i, o, u or a silent h: write j’ glued to the verb, with no space.
Keep the je ending -e on the verb itself.
watch: The apostrophe replaces the e: j’arrive, never je’arrive and never j’ arrive.
The elision changes nothing else: the ending stays -e for je.

sections.title: -ger and -cer: what happens with nous
sections.text: Before o, a g and a c would harden. The nous form of these verbs adds a letter so the verb keeps the sound of its infinitive.

rows: the e keeps the g soft
the e keeps the g soft
the e keeps the g soft
the e keeps the g soft
the cedilla keeps the c soft
the cedilla keeps the c soft
the cedilla keeps the c soft

steps: Check the infinitive: does it end in -ger or in -cer?
-ger: keep an e before -ons.
-cer: put a cedilla on the c before -ons.
Only the nous form changes; je, tu, il, vous and ils are spelled as usual.
watch: The e and the cedilla are not endings: the ending is still -ons.
Do not swap the two tricks: manger never takes a cedilla, commencer never takes an e there.

sections.title: Verbs that take è: acheter, lever, préférer
sections.text: When the ending is silent (je, tu, il/elle, ils/elles), the last vowel of the stem is stressed and written with a grave accent. With nous and vous the ending is heard and the stem goes back to the spelling of the infinitive.
steps: Write the ending first and ask: is it silent (-e, -es, -ent) or heard (-ons, -ez)?
Silent ending: put a grave accent on the last vowel of the stem.
Heard ending: keep the infinitive spelling.
In préférer and espérer only the second accent moves; the first é never changes.
watch: Four persons out of six take the accent; nous and vous are the two exceptions.
The accent and the elision are separate things: j’achète needs both.

sections.title: Verbs that double a letter: appeler, jeter
sections.text: Same idea, different spelling: before a silent ending appeler doubles its l and jeter doubles its t. Before -ons and -ez the letter stays single.
steps: Write the ending and ask whether it is silent or pronounced.
Silent ending: double the last consonant of the stem.
-ons or -ez: keep a single consonant, as in the infinitive.
watch: The doubling never reaches nous and vous.
The endings themselves do not change: -e, -es, -ent as usual.

sections.title: payer: two spellings are allowed
sections.text: Before a silent ending, payer may change its y into i. Both spellings are correct. Before -ons and -ez the y always stays.

rows: -ons is heard, so the y stays
-ez is heard, so the y stays

steps: Find the subject and write its ending.
Silent ending: write the stem with y or with i, both count.
-ons or -ez: keep the y.
watch: There is no form with i before -ons or -ez.
Pick one spelling and keep it in the same sentence.

sections.title: After aimer: a verb or a noun
sections.text: Aimer is followed either by a verb in the infinitive, with no word for “to”, or by a noun with le, la or les in front of it.
steps: Decide what follows: an action or a thing.
An action: leave that verb in its dictionary form, with no preposition.
A thing: put le, la or les in front of it, even when English has no word there.
Only aimer carries the subject’s ending.
watch: Two conjugated verbs in a row is the classic slip: aimons cuisinons is impossible.
Du chocolat means some chocolate; liking it in general takes a different article.

steps: Find the subject, then remove -er from the infinitive.
Take the ending written on that subject’s row.
Check the ending really belongs to that person: -ons only with nous, -ez only with vous.
Ask whether the subject is several people: ils, elles, or a plural noun.
Write the plural ending even though you hear nothing.
It is spelled with -ent; -ont belongs to avoir, être and faire.
Look at the first sound of the verb, not at its meaning.
Vowel or silent h: replace the e of je with an apostrophe and glue it to the verb.
Keep the je ending on the verb itself.
Check that the infinitive ends in -ger.
For nous, keep the e of the stem before -ons so the g stays soft.
Spell every other person normally.
Check that the infinitive ends in -cer.
For nous, put a cedilla under the c before -ons.
Do not add an e as well: that trick belongs to -ger verbs.
Write the ending first and ask whether it is silent.
Silent ending: put a grave accent on the last vowel of the stem.
Heard ending (-ons, -ez): keep the spelling of the infinitive.
Write the ending and ask whether it is silent.
Silent ending: double the last consonant of the stem.
-ons or -ez: keep a single consonant.
Find the subject and write its ending.
Silent ending: the y may become i, and both spellings count.
-ons or -ez: keep the y.
Conjugate only aimer, for its own subject.
If an action follows, leave it in the infinitive with no preposition.
If a thing follows, put le, la or les in front of it.

exercises.hint: Start from the stem parl-. Which ending goes with vous?
exercises.feedback: Remove -er and add the vous ending.
exercises.explanation: Vous parlez: parl- + -ez.

mistakes.why: Parles is the tu ending, for one person you are close to. The subject asked for is the polite or plural you.
Parle is the je and il/elle form, one single person. The subject here is a different person of the verb.
Parlons is the nous form: it includes the speaker. Vous is the group you are speaking to, not the one you belong to.
Parlent is the ils/elles ending, for people you are talking about, not for people you address.
Parler is the infinitive, the dictionary form. A subject needs a conjugated ending instead of -er.

exercises.hint: The tu ending is silent but written.
exercises.feedback: Tu forms of -er verbs end in -es.
exercises.explanation: Tu regardes: regard- + -es.

mistakes.why: That is the je and il/elle form. Tu has a written ending of its own, even though it sounds exactly the same.
Regardez is the vous ending, for the polite or plural you. Tu is one person you know well.
Regardent is the ils/elles ending, for several people.
Regardons is the nous form and includes the speaker; the subject here is only tu.
Regarder is the infinitive. Once a subject is there, the verb has to carry an ending.

exercises.hint: Look for the nous ending.
exercises.feedback: Nous forms end in -ons.
exercises.explanation: Nous jouons: jou- + -ons.

mistakes.why: Jouez is the vous ending: it speaks to other people. Nous means we, the group the speaker belongs to.
Jouent is the ils/elles ending, for people being talked about, not for a group that includes the speaker.
Joue is the je and il/elle form, one single person. Nous is plural and has its own ending.

exercises.hint: Plural you is vous. Pick its ending.
exercises.feedback: One verb tile has the ils ending.
exercises.explanation: Vous travaillez: travaill- + -ez.

mistakes.why: Travaillent is the ils/elles ending, for people you talk about. The subject tile addresses them directly, so the verb needs the matching ending.
Travailler needs à in front of a town: working somewhere is never expressed without it.

exercises.hint: The il ending of -er verbs is the same as the je ending. Languages are lowercase.
exercises.feedback: Use the il form of parler.
exercises.explanation: Il parle espagnol: parl- + -e. Il parle l’espagnol is also correct.

mistakes.why: Parles is the tu ending. Il is one person being talked about, so the verb takes the third-person ending.
Espagnole with an e is the feminine adjective, as in une chanteuse espagnole. The language itself is not spelled that way.
En espagnol means “in Spanish”, the language something is said in. Naming the language you speak needs no en.
Le cannot stay whole in front of a vowel; it loses its e and takes an apostrophe.

exercises.instruction: Change je to vous and adjust the verb.
exercises.hint: Swap the je ending for the vous ending.
exercises.feedback: The vous form ends in -ez.
exercises.explanation: Vous chantez bien: chant- + -ez.

mistakes.why: Chante is the je and il/elle form, one single person. The new subject is plural or polite you.
Chantes is the tu ending, for one person you know well, not for the subject you were asked to use.
Chantent is the ils/elles ending, for people being talked about, not for people being addressed.
Chantons is the nous form and includes the speaker. The subject changed to the person spoken to.

exercises.hint: Mes parents means ils. Which ending goes with ils?
exercises.feedback: The ils ending of -er verbs is written -ent and is silent.
exercises.explanation: Mes parents habitent: habit- + -ent.

mistakes.why: There is no -ont ending on -er verbs. You are thinking of ils ont and ils sont, which belong to avoir and être.
Habites is the tu ending, for one person. Mes parents is several people.
Habitez is the vous ending, used when you speak to people. Here the people are being talked about.

exercises.hint: The elles ending is silent but has three letters.
exercises.feedback: Elles takes the same ending as ils.
exercises.explanation: Elles écoutent: écout- + -ent.

mistakes.why: That is the je and il/elle form, one person. Elles is plural, and the plural ending is longer even though it sounds the same.
Écoutes is the tu ending, for one person you know well.
Écoutons is the nous form: it includes the speaker, which elles does not.
Écoutez is the vous ending, addressed to someone. Elles are being talked about.
There is no -ont ending on -er verbs; -ont belongs to ils ont and ils font.

exercises.hint: -ons belongs to nous.
exercises.feedback: Ils needs its own ending.
exercises.explanation: Ils dansent: the ils ending is -ent, and it is silent.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Dansons is the nous form, which includes the speaker; the subject here is a group being talked about.
Danse is the singular form. Ils is plural and adds a written ending you cannot hear.
-ont is not an -er ending; it belongs to ils ont and ils sont.
That changes the subject instead of the verb, and the instruction is to keep ils.
Dansez is the vous ending, used when speaking to people, not when talking about them.

exercises.instruction: Change il to ils and adjust the verb.
exercises.hint: The verb sounds the same, but the spelling changes.
exercises.feedback: Add the written plural ending to the verb.
exercises.explanation: Ils regardent: regarde and regardent sound the same, but ils needs -ent.

mistakes.why: That is still the singular form. French writes a plural ending on the verb even when nothing changes in the sound.
Regardes is the tu ending, for one person you know well; the new subject is plural.
-ont is not an -er verb ending. It belongs to ils ont, ils sont, ils font.
The subject was left singular. Making it plural means writing its s as well as changing the verb.

exercises.hint: The ils ending is silent but written.
exercises.feedback: The ils ending of -er verbs is not -ont.
exercises.explanation: Ils donnent: donn- + -ent.

mistakes.why: -ont is not an -er ending; ont and sont are forms of avoir and être.
That is the singular form for je and il/elle. The subject asked for is plural.
Donnes is the tu ending, for one person you know well.
Donnons is the nous form and includes the speaker.
Donner is the infinitive; a subject calls for a conjugated ending.

exercises.hint: Habiter begins with a silent h.
exercises.feedback: Je changes before a vowel or a silent h, and the ending must match je.
exercises.explanation: J’habite: je becomes j’ before the silent h of habite.

mistakes.why: The h of habiter is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound. Je cannot keep its e in front of one.
The apostrophe is right, but -es is the tu ending. The subject here is the speaker.

exercises.hint: Aime begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Je cannot stay whole before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: J’aime la musique: je becomes j’ before aime.

mistakes.why: Aime begins with a vowel, so je cannot stay whole in front of it.
A French noun needs an article: liking something in general still takes le, la or les.

exercises.hint: Look at the letter that starts the verb.
exercises.feedback: Je loses its e before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: J’arrive: je becomes j’ before a vowel.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Arrive begins with a vowel, and je never stands whole in front of one.
The apostrophe is fixed, but -es is the tu ending and the subject is the speaker.
The apostrophe replaces the e of je, it is not added after it.

exercises.hint: The verb begins with a vowel, so je changes. Écouter needs no word for “to”.
exercises.feedback: Check what happens to je before écoute.
exercises.explanation: J’écoute la radio: j’ before a vowel, and écouter takes a direct object.

mistakes.why: Écoute begins with a vowel, so je has to lose its e in front of it.
Écouter takes its object directly: there is no word for “to” after it in French.
-es is the tu ending, for one person you know well; the subject is the speaker.

exercises.instruction: Write je, or its short form, as the verb needs.
exercises.hint: Oublie begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Je changes before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: J’oublie: je becomes j’ before oublie.

mistakes.why: Oublie begins with a vowel, and je drops its e in front of a vowel sound.
The apostrophe is part of the short form; the bare letter is not a word.
Only the e disappears: the apostrophe replaces it instead of being added to the whole word.

exercises.hint: Keep the g soft before -ons.
exercises.feedback: A g before o sounds hard. The nous form needs an extra letter to keep it soft.
exercises.explanation: Nous mangeons: mange- + -ons. The e keeps the g soft.

mistakes.why: With no e, the g sits straight before o and is read hard, like the g of gare. Manger sounds soft and has to stay soft.
-ont is not an -er verb ending; it belongs to ils ont and ils sont.
Mangent is the ils/elles form. The subject asked for includes the speaker.
That is the infinitive; the question asks for a form that goes with a subject.

exercises.source: Nous ____ à la piscine le mardi.
exercises.hint: Nager is a -ger verb.
exercises.feedback: The nous form of a -ger verb keeps an e before -ons.
exercises.explanation: Nous nageons: the e keeps the g soft before -ons.

mistakes.why: Dropping the e puts the g straight before o, which makes it hard, as in gomme.
-ont is not an -er verb ending; it belongs to ont and sont.
Nagent is the ils/elles form, for several people being talked about.
Nagez is the vous ending, addressed to other people; the subject here includes the speaker.

exercises.source: Nous ____ nos affaires dans le placard.
exercises.hint: Ranger is a -ger verb.
exercises.feedback: Look for the form that keeps the g soft before -ons.
exercises.explanation: Nous rangeons: -ger verbs keep an e before -ons.

mistakes.why: With no e the g comes straight before o and is pronounced hard, unlike the g of ranger.
-ont is not an -er ending; it belongs to ils ont and ils sont.

exercises.hint: Say the verb aloud: the g should sound like the g in manger.
exercises.feedback: One letter is missing before -ons.
exercises.explanation: Nous mangeons: -ger verbs keep the e before -ons.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Before o the g needs help to keep the soft sound of manger.
-ont is not an -er verb ending, and it does not belong to this subject.
Mangions is the imperfect, for something that used to happen. The sentence is in the present.

exercises.hint: Voyager is a -ger verb.
exercises.feedback: Remember the spelling of the nous form of a -ger verb.
exercises.explanation: Nous voyageons beaucoup: voyage- + -ons.

mistakes.why: Without the e the g stands before o and hardens; the soft g of voyager has to be protected.
Voyagent is the ils/elles form, for people being talked about, not for a group that includes the speaker.
Voyage is the singular form for je and il/elle; a plural subject needs its own ending.

exercises.hint: Keep the c soft before -ons.
exercises.feedback: A c before o sounds like k. The nous form needs a special c.
exercises.explanation: Nous commençons: ç keeps the soft s sound before o.

mistakes.why: A plain c before o is read like a k, so this would sound like “commenkons”. The soft c of commencer needs its hook.
Adding an e is what -ger verbs do. A c is kept soft a different way.
Commencent is the ils/elles form; the subject asked for includes the speaker.
That is the infinitive, not a form that goes with a subject.

exercises.hint: Avancer is a -cer verb.
exercises.feedback: The nous form of a -cer verb needs a cedilla.
exercises.explanation: Nous avançons: ç before -ons.

mistakes.why: A bare c before o is read like a k, which is not how avancer sounds.
The extra e is the trick of -ger verbs such as manger; a verb in -cer keeps its c soft another way.
Avancent is the ils/elles form, for several people being talked about.
Avancez is the vous ending, addressed to other people; here the speaker is part of the group.

exercises.hint: The c must sound like s.
exercises.feedback: Before o, a plain c sounds like k.
exercises.explanation: Nous commençons: ç keeps the soft sound.

mistakes.why: Before o a bare c sounds like k, so this would be read “commenkons”.
An e before -ons is what -ger verbs need. A c is softened with a different mark.

exercises.instruction: Change je to nous and adjust the verb.
exercises.source: Je place les verres sur la table.
answers: Nous plaçons les verres sur la table.
exercises.hint: Placer is a -cer verb.
exercises.feedback: The nous form of placer needs a cedilla.
exercises.explanation: Nous plaçons: -cer verbs write ç before -ons.

answers: Nous placons les verres sur la table.
mistakes.why: The c before o would be read like a k; placer keeps a soft c in every form.

answers: Nous placeons les verres sur la table.
mistakes.why: The added e belongs to -ger verbs such as manger, not to a verb in -cer.

answers: Nous place les verres sur la table.
mistakes.why: Place is the je and il/elle form; the new subject is plural and needs its own ending.

answers: Nous plaçont les verres sur la table.
mistakes.why: -ont is not an -er verb ending; it belongs to ont and sont.

alternatives.message: The verb form is right, but je becomes j’ before a vowel: j’achète.

exercises.hint: The stem changes when the ending is silent. Watch the elision too.
exercises.feedback: The e before t needs an accent in the je form.
exercises.explanation: J’achète: è before a silent ending, and je becomes j’.

mistakes.why: The ending is silent, so the e of the stem carries the sound and is pronounced open. French marks that sound with an accent.
-es is the tu ending, for one person you know well; the subject asked for is the speaker.
Achetons is the plural form that includes the speaker, and its ending is heard, so its stem stays plain.
That is the infinitive; the question asks for a form that goes with a subject.

exercises.source: Tu ____ le thé ou le café ?
exercises.hint: The second accent changes in the tu form.
exercises.feedback: Préférer changes one of its accents before a silent ending.
exercises.explanation: Tu préfères: the second é becomes è.

mistakes.why: The ending is silent here, so the second vowel of the stem is stressed and cannot keep the closed accent of the infinitive.
That is the je and il/elle form. Tu adds a written ending you cannot hear.
Préférons is the form for the group including the speaker, and its ending is heard, so both accents stay as in the infinitive.
Préférez is the vous ending, polite or plural; tu is one person you know well.

exercises.hint: Lever changes its stem before a silent ending.
exercises.feedback: The il/elle form of lever needs an accent.
exercises.explanation: Elle lève la main: e becomes è before a silent ending.

mistakes.why: With no accent the e before v is read weak and almost silent. Before a silent ending that vowel is stressed and must be marked.
Lèvent is the ils/elles form, for several people. Elle is one person.

exercises.source: Ils achetent des fruits au marché.
answers: Ils achètent des fruits au marché.
exercises.hint: The ils ending is silent, so the stem changes.
exercises.feedback: A letter in the stem needs an accent.
exercises.explanation: Ils achètent: è before the silent -ent.

answers: Ils achetent des fruits au marché.
mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. The -ent ending is silent, so the e of the stem carries the sound and needs its mark.

answers: Ils achètes des fruits au marché.
mistakes.why: -es is the tu ending, for one person you know well; the subject is plural.

answers: Ils achète des fruits au marché.
mistakes.why: That is the singular form. A plural subject also needs the written plural ending.

exercises.hint: With nous, the ending is not silent.
exercises.feedback: The nous form keeps the accents of the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Nous préférons: no stem change with nous, so both accents stay é.

mistakes.why: The grave accent appears only when the ending is silent. This ending is pronounced, so the stem keeps the accents of the infinitive.
Préférer keeps both of its accents in this form; without them the word is read differently.
Préférez is the vous ending, for the people you address, not for the group that includes the speaker.
Plage is feminine: une plage, so the article is wrong.

alternatives.message: The verb form is right, but je becomes j’ before a vowel: j’appelle.

exercises.hint: Appeler doubles a letter before a silent ending. Watch the elision.
exercises.feedback: The l doubles in the je form.
exercises.explanation: J’appelle: ll before the silent -e, and je becomes j’.

mistakes.why: A single l is the spelling used when the ending is heard. Before a silent ending the stem of appeler is written stronger.
-es is the tu ending, for one person you know well; the question asks for the speaker.
Appelons is the plural form including the speaker, and its ending is pronounced, so its stem keeps one l.
That is the infinitive, not a form that goes with a subject.

exercises.hint: Jeter doubles a letter before a silent ending.
exercises.feedback: The t doubles in the ils form.
exercises.explanation: Ils jettent: tt before the silent -ent.

mistakes.why: One t is the spelling used when the ending is heard. This ending is silent, so the stem of jeter is written stronger.
That is the singular form, for je and il/elle. A plural subject adds a written plural ending.
-es is the tu ending, for one person you know well.
-ont is not an -er verb ending; it belongs to ont and sont.
Jetons is the form for the group including the speaker, and its ending is pronounced, so the t stays single.

exercises.hint: With nous, the ending is not silent.
exercises.feedback: The doubling only happens before a silent ending.
exercises.explanation: Nous appelons: one l, because -ons is pronounced.

mistakes.why: The doubling happens only when the ending is silent. This ending is pronounced, so the stem keeps its infinitive spelling.
Appelez is the vous ending, addressed to other people. The subject here includes the speaker.

exercises.hint: Jeter doubles its consonant before a silent ending.
exercises.feedback: One verb tile is missing a letter.
exercises.explanation: Je jette: tt before the silent -e.

mistakes.why: A single t belongs to the forms whose ending is heard. Here the ending is silent, so the stem is written stronger.
Le is the article of ballon and stays in front of it. Put before the verb, le becomes a pronoun meaning “it”, and the noun is left bare.

exercises.instruction: Change nous to elle and adjust the verb.
exercises.hint: The ending becomes silent, so the stem changes.
exercises.feedback: Appeler doubles its l before a silent ending.
exercises.explanation: Elle appelle un taxi: ll before the silent -e.

mistakes.why: A single l goes with the forms whose ending is heard. The new ending is silent, so the stem changes.
-es is the tu ending, for the person you are talking to; elle is a person being talked about.
That still carries the plural ending of the old subject, which included the speaker.

exercises.hint: Payer has two accepted spellings in this form.
exercises.feedback: Before a silent ending, payer can change one letter.
exercises.explanation: Je paie (or je paye): y can become i before a silent ending.

mistakes.why: -es is the tu ending, for one person you know well; the question asks for the speaker.
-ent is the ils/elles ending, for several people.
Payons is the plural form including the speaker, and its ending is pronounced.
That is the infinitive; a subject calls for a conjugated form.

exercises.hint: Before a silent ending, payer may change a letter.
exercises.feedback: Use the tu ending -es.
exercises.explanation: Tu paies (or tu payes): both spellings are correct.

mistakes.why: Those are the je and il/elle forms. Tu adds a written ending that you cannot hear.
Payez is the vous ending, polite or plural; tu is one person you know well.
-ent is the ils/elles ending, for several people.
Payons is the form for a group including the speaker, and its ending is pronounced.

exercises.hint: With nous, the ending is pronounced.
exercises.feedback: The y changes only before a silent ending.
exercises.explanation: Nous payons: y stays before -ons.

mistakes.why: The y turns into i only before a silent ending. This ending is pronounced, so the stem keeps its y.
Paient is the ils/elles form, for several people being talked about.

exercises.hint: Payer may change a letter before the silent ils ending.
exercises.feedback: Use the ils form of payer.
exercises.explanation: Ils paient le loyer (or ils payent): both spellings are correct.

mistakes.why: That is the singular form, for one person. The subject is plural and needs the written plural ending.
Payez is the vous ending, used when speaking to people; here they are being talked about.
Loyer is masculine: un loyer, le loyer, so the article does not fit.

exercises.hint: After aimer, the second verb is not conjugated.
exercises.feedback: Look for the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Elle aime danser: aimer + infinitive.

mistakes.why: Danse is a conjugated form (je danse, elle danse). Two conjugated verbs cannot follow each other here.
Dansé is the past participle, used with avoir for something already done: elle a dansé.

exercises.hint: Only one verb is conjugated.
exercises.feedback: The verb after aimer stays in the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Nous aimons cuisiner: aimons is conjugated, cuisiner stays in the infinitive.

mistakes.why: The second tile is conjugated for the subject. Only the first verb of the pair carries the subject’s ending.
The first verb is the one that must show the subject and the tense; left in its dictionary form it shows neither.

exercises.hint: After aimer, a noun needs an article even when English has none.
exercises.feedback: Use the definite article before chocolat.
exercises.explanation: J’aime le chocolat: aimer + le/la/les when talking about things in general.

mistakes.why: A French noun cannot stand bare after the verb; it needs an article even where English has none.
Aime starts with a vowel, so je has to lose its e in front of it.
Du chocolat means some chocolate, a quantity of it. Liking something in general points at the thing as a whole.
-es is the tu ending, for the person you are talking to; the subject here is the speaker.

exercises.hint: After aimer, use the infinitive, with no word for “to”.
exercises.feedback: Do not conjugate the second verb.
exercises.explanation: Il aime nager: aimer + infinitive.

mistakes.why: Nage is a conjugated form (je nage, il nage). After aimer the second verb keeps its dictionary form.
No preposition comes between aimer and the following verb; the English “to” has no equivalent here.
Aimer takes the next verb directly, with no de and no other little word.
-es is the tu ending, for the person you are talking to; il is a person being talked about.

exercises.hint: Something is missing before chocolat.
exercises.feedback: After aimer, a noun takes a definite article.
exercises.explanation: Tu aimes le chocolat ? Aimer + le/la/les + noun.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. A noun cannot stand alone after aimer in French.
Du chocolat is some chocolate, a portion of it. Saying what you like in general points at the thing as a whole.
Un chocolat is one single chocolate, an item you could count, not chocolate in general.
The article is fixed, but the verb lost its tu ending: tu always writes -es on an -er verb.

exercises.instruction: Write the right form of voyager.
exercises.hint: Aimez is already conjugated.
exercises.feedback: The second verb stays in the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Vous aimez voyager ? Aimer + infinitive.

mistakes.why: Aimez already carries the vous ending. The second verb does not repeat it.
Voyage is a conjugated form (je voyage, il voyage). After aimer the verb stays in its dictionary form.
Voyagé is the past participle, for something already done: vous avez voyagé.
Aimer is followed by the next verb directly; the English “to” has no equivalent here.
